Depth options
Model and methodology

Depth and binocular correspondence

An autostereogram encodes depth through horizontal repetition. Each eye matches a different repetition of the same texture. The editor combines shapes, text and painted depth into a relative depth map, then constrains matching pixels to have the same colour. Texture colour itself does not encode depth.

Geometry and rendering

Depth z runs from 0 (far) to 1 (near). Let R be the background repeat in output pixels. If the depth-strength control reads P percent, a = 0.2 × P / 100. For parallel viewing, μ = 2a / (1 + a) and the pixel separation is:

s(z) = round[2R(1 − μz) / (2 − μz)]

Cross-eyed viewing uses μ = 2a / (3 + a) and replaces (1 − μz) with (1 + μz). Nearer surfaces then have a larger separation. The renderer applies symmetric colour constraints row by row and tests for hidden surfaces before linking pixels. Image generation runs in a worker; editing previews use fewer pixels than a full-resolution export.

Interpretation and limits

Depth is relative, not a distance measurement. Whole-pixel disparities can flatten fine depth changes, especially in small exports. Check detail marks changes that disappear at the chosen resolution. Photograph-based depth estimates are predictions, not measured geometry; their optional model runs locally after its first download. Design and Depth map provide direct views of the scene even when the stereoscopic effect is difficult to see.

Reference

Harold Thimbleby, Ian Witten and Stuart Inglis, “Displaying 3D Images: Algorithms for Single-Image Random-Dot Stereograms” (1994). The editor adapts its correspondence and hidden-surface method with adjustable depth strength and a cross-eyed viewing mode. See Help for editing controls and Viewing help for viewing practice.

Get started

  1. Build your design. Add a shape, type some text or import a photo. Drag an object to move it; use its handles to resize.
  2. Choose a texture. Open Stereogram and choose a pattern or your own image. Hold Reveal to check the hidden shape.
  3. See the depth. Use Viewing help to practise, then Export to save your image.
